subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Latin America Reading
subtitle: Location, environments, people, resources, and sustainability across Latin America
description: A reading pack with source-faithful passages on Latin America as a region, its physical geography, urbanization, resources, hazards, and sustainability trade-offs.

data.sourceTitle: What Makes Latin America a Region?
data.targetTitle: What Makes Latin America a Region?
data.sourcePassage: Latin America is a large and diverse world region. It usually includes Mexico, Central America, much of South America, and many islands in the Caribbean Sea. The region is often connected by location, colonial history, and languages such as Spanish and Portuguese. Brazil is the largest Portuguese-speaking country in the region, while Spanish is widely spoken in many other countries. However, Latin America should not be treated as one single type of place. It includes rainforests, deserts, mountains, islands, grasslands, megacities, rural communities, Indigenous cultures, Afro-Latin American heritage, and many mixed identities. A region is a human-made idea that helps geographers organize information. The borders of a region can change depending on whether the question is about language, physical geography, history, trade, or culture.

data.sourcePassage: Latin America has varied physical geography. The Andes Mountains run along the western edge of South America through countries such as Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina. The Amazon Basin is a huge lowland region drained by the Amazon River and its tributaries. It contains the Amazon Rainforest, which stores carbon, influences rainfall, and supports great biodiversity. The Atacama Desert in northern Chile and southern Peru is one of the driest places on Earth, yet mining, astronomy, tourism, and some specialized farming occur there. Climate changes across the region because of latitude, altitude, landforms, and ocean currents. In the Andes, higher altitude usually means cooler temperatures. The cold Humboldt Current helps create dry conditions along parts of the Pacific coast. El Nino can disrupt normal ocean and weather patterns.

data.sourcePassage: Population in Latin America is not evenly spread. Many people live in cities, coastal areas, valleys, and highland basins. Fewer people live in dense rainforest, deserts, very high mountains, or remote interior areas. Major cities include Mexico City, Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Buenos Aires, Lima, Bogota, and Santiago. During the 20th and 21st centuries, many cities grew rapidly as people moved from rural areas and smaller towns to places with jobs, schools, hospitals, transport, and services. This urban growth can create opportunities, but it also creates challenges. Cities may face traffic congestion, air pollution, water supply problems, housing shortages, informal settlements, and inequality. Physical setting matters too. Mexico City is in a highland basin where polluted air can become trapped, while Lima is on a dry Pacific coast where water scarcity is a concern.

data.sourcePassage: Latin America has many natural resources. Brazil has forests, iron ore, farmland, and water resources. Chile and Peru are important copper producers. Venezuela has large oil reserves. Mexico has oil, manufacturing, agriculture, and tourism. Peru has minerals and fishing resources, while many Caribbean islands rely on tourism, services, agriculture, and ports. Resources can help countries earn money, create jobs, build infrastructure, and trade with other regions. However, relying too much on one resource can be risky if prices fall. Resource use can also damage environments. Copper mining can use water and change landscapes, oil can cause pollution, tourism can pressure reefs and water supplies, and farming can lead to soil erosion. Sustainability asks how communities can improve quality of life while protecting land, water, ecosystems, and future needs.

data.sourcePassage: Geography helps explain why some places face hazards and how human choices affect risk. Many Caribbean islands lie in warm tropical waters where hurricanes can form. Storms may damage homes, roads, airports, farms, coral reefs, and power systems. However, a hurricane does not have to become a disaster. Strong buildings, early warning systems, evacuation plans, emergency supplies, healthy wetlands, and fair access to help can reduce risk. In the Amazon, deforestation often spreads outward from roads. Roads make it easier for logging, ranching, farming, mining, and settlement to enter forest areas. Forest clearing can create jobs and income for some people, but it can also cause habitat loss, carbon release, soil erosion, rainfall changes, and threats to Indigenous land rights. Sustainable decisions require comparing benefits, harms, and long-term consequences.

questions.question: Why is Amazon deforestation both an environmental and economic issue?

Using every resource as quickly as possible
